movement.text: The port of Adulis connected a highland center to Red Sea exchange.

evidence.text: Architecture, inscriptions and coinage reveal different periods; Roman glass offers material evidence that must be tied to find context.

authority.text: Royal inscriptions make claims in particular languages and scripts. The inland excavation supplies different evidence for work and local change; neither establishes every resident’s identity or beliefs.

coordination.text: A highland center, coastal outlet and inland production/consumption sites performed different tasks. Named exchange points do not by themselves reconstruct a particular trader’s route.

name: Aksum and Adulis
place: Northern Ethiopia and Eritrea; Red Sea connections
geographicPrecision: Aksum city locator; Adulis is a distinct coastal port.

interval.label: 1st–8th centuries CE
interval.note: Broad conventional flourishing in the consulted architectural essay; not exact founding and extinction.

question: How could an inland city connect to the sea?
summary: Aksum’s highland city, Adulis on the Red Sea and an inland town did different work in a connected economy. A merchant-oriented text describes exchange; excavated food-processing equipment, craft debris and coins reveal activities away from the capital’s monuments. These sources also belong to different centuries. The early port account, later royal inscriptions and Beta Samati’s late deposits should be compared through time, rather than assembled into one scene at 200 CE.

sections.title: The inland city was not itself a harbor
sections.text: The first-century Periplus describes Adulis and an inland connection to Aksum. Binyam and Krebs explain how this merchant-oriented account links a coastal outlet with inland exchange and distinguishes goods for different buyers. It is not simply a list of royal luxuries. The account’s identification of a ruler called Zoskales is debated; the passage cannot define precise first-century imperial borders. The map therefore separates the highland city, the port and a later archaeological research area, without tracing one ship’s voyage or an exact mountain road.

citations.locator: Excerpt pp. 5–7: Periplus, Adulis and Zoskales

sections.title: Inland work sustained more than monuments
sections.text: At Beta Samati, excavators found food-storage and preparation evidence alongside small-scale metal and glass-working debris in Area A. Grinding stones, ordinary pottery and changes in the use of a space make recurring work visible. The authors interpret slag and glass wasters as evidence of production. These findings complicate the assumption that all glass in the region was imported. They come from a particular town and dated layers, not a census of every Aksumite household. The nearby basilica belongs to another area and a sequence of building phases.

citations.locator: Printed pp. 1540–1543: methods, Area A and selected Area B

sections.title: An old coin can occur in a later deposit
sections.text: The reproduced excavation photograph presents five coins, each shown on two sides. They include different rulers and dates, not five contemporary issues. The authors combine coin identification with pottery and radiocarbon evidence when interpreting the upper deposits. A coin’s manufacture, use, deposition and modern excavation are separate events. An older specimen does not automatically date an entire layer, and the photograph alone cannot establish how long each coin circulated. The published chronology for Armah is itself discussed with an alternative; the account does not turn that debate into a single secure year.

citations.locator: Printed pp. 1541–1542, Figure 4 and Armah chronology

sections.title: Royal language and local change need separate clocks
sections.text: Fourth-century royal inscriptions use Greek and Ge’ez in more than one script. Binyam and Krebs distinguish language from script and warn that the ancient name Ethiopia had shifting uses. A royal conversion also does not identify every resident’s beliefs. Coins, inscriptions, domestic material and the basilica illuminate different changes. The older Roman grape-shaped bottle remains a type comparison: this museum specimen is not documented as excavated at Aksum. The new excavation photograph supplies a different kind of evidence with an actual reported find context.

deeperReading.title: A building plan is not a single frozen household
deeperReading.text: The excavators distinguish Area A’s residential/workshop activities from Area B’s basilica and identify phases within them. Because walls continue into unexcavated ground, they use space rather than assuming every enclosed-looking area was a complete room. This matters when explaining who cooked, stored goods or made things: an excavated assemblage has a location and history, but it is not an unposed portrait of one family. The study also reports food consumption near the basilica. Sacred, administrative and ordinary activities can intersect without becoming identical. More work is needed before assigning specific households or a complete production organization.

deeperReading.title: Inscription, copy and modern interpretation are distinct sources
deeperReading.text: Binyam and Krebs discuss two different Adulis monuments whose texts survive through Cosmas’s later account. One commemorated a Hellenistic ruler; another recorded the claims of an Aksumite ruler centuries later. They should not become one monument, one king or a contemporary first-century witness. Their discussion also distinguishes two languages from three scripts in fourth-century royal texts, refining an older museum shorthand. The excerpt consulted here is only eight pages of a larger book. Its discussion of political claims should not be converted into exact boundaries, universal language use or a history of all communities in the region.

familyActivity.title: Give a coin more than one date
steps: In the excavation image, find five columns. Each pairs two views of a coin; do not count the ten photographs as ten objects.
Use the evidence note to separate an older coin from the later deposits discussed by the excavators.
Put these actions in a possible order: a coin is made, used, enters the ground, and is excavated and photographed. Explain what the image alone leaves unknown.
familyActivity.explanation: The figure was published in 2019; the coins and deposits are much older. Dates of manufacture and context must be read together. The exercise does not supply an exact circulation history for any specimen.

evidenceReading.title: Exchange, manufacture and find context
evidenceReading.introduction: These are paraphrases of the consulted scholarship, not newly translated ancient texts or an independent reanalysis of the excavation.

items.label: A port account has a particular audience
items.text: The Periplus discussion describes Adulis in a merchant-oriented account, including goods for different buyers and links inland.
items.interpretation: It is a first-century witness, not a description of every later phase. Zoskales’s relationship to Aksum remains uncertain.

items.label: Production leaves material traces
items.text: The excavators report metal slag and glass wasters in Area A alongside domestic material.
items.interpretation: This supports local work at Beta Samati and challenges treating every glass item as an import. It does not identify the origin of every glass object in the kingdom.

items.label: Five coins have different histories
items.text: From left to right the source identifies Armah, Armah, an anonymous ruler, pre-Christian Ezana and MHDYS. Coin types are considered with pottery and radiocarbon dates.
items.interpretation: These coins are not one issue of 200 CE. The authors discuss late upper deposits and alternative Armah dating; the picture is not a self-sufficient layer date.

limitations: Only the eight-page Binyam/Krebs excerpt was consulted, not the full book or complete critical Periplus edition.
Excavation associations, radiocarbon calibration, coin chronology and all original inscriptions were not independently reanalysed.
More agricultural, regional, gender and enslavement evidence and independent review remain.

placeStudy.title: Aksum: highland city, coastal outlet and inland research
placeStudy.description: Approximate locators distinguish different functions and dates. The Yeha-district point orients the Beta Samati discussion; it is not the exact excavation coordinate. The map draws no precise mountain road or territorial boundary and does not make later deposits contemporary with the first-century port account.

points.label: Aksum — highland center
points.text: The capital locator is inland. Its connection with Adulis does not make Aksum a coastal harbor, nor date every surviving monument to 200 CE.

points.label: Adulis — Red Sea outlet
points.text: Binyam and Krebs place Adulis near the Gulf of Zula and discuss the Periplus’s port/inland connection. Ancient landing places and shorelines require separate archaeological investigation.

points.label: Yeha district — Beta Samati research area
points.text: The excavators locate Beta Samati northeast of Yeha and document multiple periods. This rounded district locator is not a surveyed excavation point or a claim that every shipment passed through the town.
